title: Peter Thiel on PayPal, contrarian truths, stagnation and the education bubble (Kristol, 2014)
summary: In a 2014 conversation with Bill Kristol, Thiel explains how PayPal won through compounding growth, a fraud-fighting technology edge and a long-term plan, and why good businesses avoid competition. He argues conformity drives bubbles, technological stagnation is largely cultural and regulatory, and higher education is a zero-sum tournament bubble.

principles.text: Good businesses avoid excess competition; they are unique, not one of many doing the same thing.
principles.quote: Well, I do think in business one of the critical things is that you don’t want excess competition.

principles.text: Being the last mover matters more than being first, and durability is as important as growth.
principles.quote: In practice, I think it’s more important to be the last mover than the first mover.

principles.text: Most business value lies far in the future, so durability is at least as important as growth.
principles.quote: Durability is at least as important as growth.

principles.text: Have a definite long-term plan rather than iterating randomly; a bad plan beats no plan.
principles.quote: When I was a chess player, an intermediate level chess lesson was always that a bad plan was better than no plan.

principles.text: Ask for a truth few people agree with; conventional thinking is powerful and bubbles come from deferring to others.
principles.quote: Tell me something that’s true that very few people agree with you on.

principles.text: Stagnation outside computing stems largely from regulation and culture; fight it rather than accept or deny it.
principles.quote: I tend to think that we live in a world where bits are quite unregulated, atoms are very heavily regulated.
